en: Furthermore, a practitioner of mantra should not commit suicide out of a desire for results, nor should he voluntarily cast off his body when suffering arises. || 1 ||
When one has attained detachment, whether after having experienced worldly enjoyments or otherwise,
one should renounce by means of meditation and concentration, with the mind dissolved in Śiva.
Having personally enumerated sound and the other [objects], as well as their respective means, [he perceives] the body, the collection of sense organs, and the stainless abode of the enjoyer. (3)
Then, having assumed the body of Śiva and having worshipped Śiva with devotion,
one should take recourse to a seat prepared of kuśa grass, consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Then, relying on the concentration (dhāraṇā) of Īśānī, having performed all that is taught by others,
one should draw the wind residing in the skull and lead it through the upper path.
By that path one should always go to Soma, Agni, the supreme Śiva—
the immovable, all-pervading God, the end of all, whose face is turned in every direction.

Because of its own true nature residing within that [receptacle], it is not perceived as being identical with it, just as water that has entered the salt ocean is not perceived as such when it has reached that salty sea. || 7 ||
By this sequential yoga, one should abandon this body—which is impermanent, the locus of all sufferings, and loathsome—from desire. 8.
Once that twice-born man has passed away,
the wise preceptor, having purified himself, should perform his funeral rites according to the rules outside the dwelling.
Having approached a pure place, one should smear it with cow-dung;
there one should worship Śiva, and then Śivāgni to the south.
Having brought the corpse, which has been rubbed with earth, ashes, and cow dung, and purified with abundant water-washing,
one should place it to the south of that fire.
Then, having sprinkled [the site] and scattered [ashes], one should meditate on the Praṇava in the heart;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worshipped [the deity], one should then commence the fire sacrifice (homa). || 12 ||
Having meditated upon Śiva by means of the path of the word, one should offer him to the God:
"O Blessed One, accept this great oblation of my own body. 13.
Having spoken thus and bid farewell to the god Śiva who resides in both,
one should then lead the fire, provided with abundant fuel, to the funeral pyre.
Having bathed and then offered water, one should bathe again and mutter the Śiva-mantras,
beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Netra, for the purification of the rites of the disciple.

Those who are related to the guru through the exclusive relationship of teacher and disciple, as well as those who are related to the guru by other ties, shall suspend for three days all ritual acts other than the obligatory ones, such as the recitation of mantras (japa) and so forth. || 16 ||

Others than them, whether householders or even those who are not householders, who abide on the path of Śiva, shall observe impurity for the death of a child for one day, being initiated therein. || 17 ||
Householders who abide by the path of the world should not transgress worldly conduct;
therefore, those who have been consecrated should observe the practices of worldly convention.

Furthermore, one who follows the path taught in the scriptures of Śiva should not consume any substance that is a source of obstruction, such as food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka) or prohibited grain, just as one avoids forbidden rice. 19.
Thus, the rite for the last journey has been briefly described by me;
now, O you of firm vows, hear concerning the mental sacrifice.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the funeral rites, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
